text: It is 2000. You run Blockbuster, with thousands of video shops across America. A small startup called Netflix rents DVDs by post. It is losing money, and its founders have come to see you.
Netflix wants Blockbuster to buy it for $50 million. Your stores bring in billions in revenue. Netflix has never made a profit.
What do you say?
Ask yourself what customers might want in five years, not what they want today.
Our estimate: your own online service starts small and slow, because store managers see it as a threat. But you learn about online rental years earlier than you otherwise would.

You saw the shift and started learning, which was smart. But building from zero is slower than buying a team that already knows how. What would have worked: Buy the startup for a small price, keep its team, and let it run separately from the stores.
Our estimate: for a small sum, for a company your size,, you own the most promising rental startup in America. Its team keeps building, away from the stores, and you now have a foot in the future.
$50 million was small for a company your size. Buying a fast-learning team is cheap insurance against your own business being disrupted.

Blockbuster said no. Netflix was losing money at the time, and according to one of its founders, Blockbuster saw it as a small niche business. Blockbuster did not launch its own online rental service in the US until August 2004.

Judging a startup only by its size today hides the real question: is it learning something your customers will want? What would have worked: Buy it cheaply and let it run on its own, or at least start your own online rental service right away.
Our estimate: it is 2004, your Netflix team is growing fast, and more people rent DVDs online every month. Your stores still bring in most of the money, but sales in them are starting to slip.
It is 2004. Blockbuster has over 9,000 stores and $6.1 billion in revenue. But in the first half of the year, sales in your existing stores fell 5.1%, and renting DVDs online is growing fast.
Your Netflix team wants more money to grow. Your store managers say online rental is stealing their customers.
Your small online service has a few loyal members. Now the market is big enough to matter.
Online rental is no longer a niche. You have no online service of your own.
What do you do about online rental?
Your stores are a strength no website has. The question is how to use them.
Our estimate: the shops look great, but each year fewer people drive to them. Online services keep growing without you.
Making the old business nicer does not stop customers moving to a new habit. What would have worked: Go online now and use your stores as something online-only rivals cannot match.

In August 2004 Blockbuster launched Blockbuster Online at $19.99 a month for three DVDs at a time, about $2 less than Netflix, with no late fees. It passed 1 million subscribers in under a year, but it was expensive: analysts expected it to add about $170 million to spending in 2005.

It was the right move, but it came four years after you turned Netflix down, and it was mostly a copy of Netflix. Being cheaper is a weak edge against a rival who got there first. What would have worked: Launch online and link it to your stores from day one, so you offer something no online-only rival can.
Our estimate: members get DVDs by post and can also return them at any store for a new movie on the spot. No online-only rival can offer that, and members flock to you.
You turned your biggest cost, thousands of stores, into a feature a website alone could not copy.

Our estimate: it is 2006, and members love swapping mailed DVDs in your stores. Blockbuster also ended late fees in January 2005, and in the first three months late-fee money fell by $128.5 million. Online is growing, but so are the costs.

It is 2006. Blockbuster ended late fees in January 2005. In the first three months, late-fee money fell by $128.5 million, and the company lost $57.5 million. In mid-2005 Netflix had about 3 million online members, against about 1 million for you.
Netflix is ahead online. You still have thousands of stores that Netflix does not.
How do you fight back?
Netflix cannot open a store tomorrow. You can let people walk into one tonight.
Our estimate: profits look better this year, but online members drift to Netflix and do not come back.

Saving cash by shrinking the part of the business that is growing only makes the shrinking part more important. What would have worked: Spend to link your stores and online service, the one thing your rival cannot copy.
Our estimate: more advertising brings some new members, but there is still no clear reason to choose you over Netflix.
Marketing a copy harder does not make it different. What would have worked: Give members something only you can offer: swap mailed DVDs in your stores.

On November 1, 2006, Blockbuster launched Total Access. Members could swap DVDs that came by post for free rentals in its stores, with plans from $5.99 a month. Subscribers grew strongly, but launch costs were higher than expected.
You finally used what Netflix did not have, your stores, to make the online service better. That is a real reason for customers to choose you.

It is 2007. Blockbuster's chief executive has left after a fight with the board over pay, and a new one takes over. Now you see the company through new eyes. From 2002 to 2005 Blockbuster lost over $4 billion. The free in-store swaps are popular, but they cost a lot of money.
Total Access is winning members from Netflix, but free in-store swaps are expensive. Investors want losses to stop.
Online is still behind Netflix, and investors want losses to stop.
What is your plan?
Cutting costs is easy. Cutting the right costs is the job.

The new CEO charged members $7 more a month for in-store swaps, and planned tests of new store layouts and of selling small electronics. Blockbuster lost 500,000 online subscribers in summer 2007, and its shares fell 17% after a November 2007 meeting with investors.

You raised the price on the one thing that made you different, just when customers were choosing between you and a rival. What would have worked: Keep the swaps cheap, close weak stores to save money, and invest the savings in movie downloads.
Our estimate: you shrink the store network carefully, keep members happy, and start building for a world where movies arrive over the internet, not on discs.
You cut the past to fund the future, and kept the feature customers loved.
Our estimate: costs fall fast, but every closed store means fewer places to swap DVDs, so online gets a little less special.
Cutting costs was needed, but you cut without a plan for what comes after discs. What would have worked: Close weak stores and put the savings into what comes next: movie downloads.
Our estimate: you moved early, used your stores as a weapon, and followed movies onto the internet. Blockbuster is still the name people think of for movie night.
Our estimate: you closed many stores, but your online service keeps a loyal group of members. Blockbuster survives as a smaller company.

In July 2010 the New York Stock Exchange stopped trading Blockbuster's shares. On September 23, 2010, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy, with its 3,000 US stores still open. In April 2011 DISH Network bought its assets for about $320 million.
Three costly calls. The board has lost its trust in you and brings in someone else.
It's 1975 and you run Kodak, the biggest name in photography. You sell the film, the chemicals and the paper. Every holiday snap in America makes you money.

In December 1975, a 25-year-old Kodak engineer named Steve Sasson finishes a strange machine: an 8-pound box that takes a 100 by 100 pixel, black-and-white picture in 23 seconds and saves it to a cassette tape. You need a TV to see it. There is no film anywhere.
It's slow, ugly and blurry. But if it ever gets good, nobody will need your film.
What do you do with the digital camera?
The film division is nervous. Whatever you pick, they'll be watching.

Kodak patents the camera, but the executives who see it are not convinced. Sasson later recalled them doubting that anyone would want to look at their pictures on a television. No digital camera goes on sale.

Protecting your best business feels safe. But a new technology that looks worse at first can still replace you, and every year you wait, someone else learns it first. What would have worked: Give digital to a small, separate team that's allowed to compete with film, and fund it from film profits.
You give Sasson twenty engineers, a separate building and one rule: don't ask the film division for permission. Film keeps paying the bills while the team learns sensors, storage and screens.
You kept the cash machine running while buying time to learn the next one. A separate team can't be strangled by the business it's meant to replace.
You rush a camera into stores. It's bulky, slow and needs a television to view anything. Almost nobody buys it, and the loss shows up in your next annual report.

Right idea, wrong year. In 1975 there were no home computers and no screens worth viewing photos on. Being first is useless if customers can't use what you sell. What would have worked: Keep developing it in a separate team, and launch when screens and storage are ready.

August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a small magnetic disk instead of film. It is not digital yet, but it needs no film, and it is on the front pages with Sony's name on it. You can still fix this.

August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Retailers panic. Your digital team isn't surprised; they've been building something similar for six years.
August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Your early camera flopped, but the world just caught up with the idea.
The board is uneasy about your last call. A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.
A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.
How do you respond to Sony?
Careful. One more bad call and the board starts asking questions about you.
Film still makes most of our money. But this time the world is watching.
The stock holds steady and the camera counters keep selling film. Inside Kodak, the message is clear: digital is not a career move. Your best engineers start taking calls from Japan.

Early versions of a disruptive product are always worse. Comparing today's quality hides the real question: how fast is it improving? What would have worked: Accept that digital is coming and start shifting money and people toward it while film is still strong.
Your market-intelligence chief, Vince Barabba, reports back: digital could replace film, but Kodak has roughly ten years to prepare. Kodak does little to prepare.

The study was right about the threat. The mistake was treating 'ten years' as permission to wait. A deadline is only useful if you start moving before it. What would have worked: Use the ten-year window to move money and talent into digital now, not in year nine.
You pull the 1975 prototype out of the cupboard and put its inventor in charge. It's six years late, but Kodak still has the money, the patents and the brand to catch up.
You announce that a growing share of film profits will fund digital imaging every year. Wall Street grumbles about lower margins. Your engineers stop job hunting.
You used the cash from the old business to pay for the new one while you still could. That's the move most incumbents make too late.
It's 2001. Your digital cameras are among the best sellers in America, and people are starting to put their photos online. Kodak has just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Digital cameras are finally taking off and Kodak is selling them, but film is still where the money is. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Kodak's new EasyShare digital cameras have made it number two in the US, but film still earns most of the money. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
Millions of people will soon put their photos online. But Kodak still earns its money from prints, paper and chemicals.
What is Ofoto for?
This is your last warning from the board. Get this one wrong and they'll find a new CEO.
Every photo that stays on a screen is a print we never sell. But maybe that's the point.
Renamed Kodak Gallery, the site grows to over 60 million users. But free accounts must keep buying prints or risk losing their photos.

You built the website around your old revenue instead of what customers wanted to do. The customer's job had changed from printing memories to sharing them. What would have worked: Make it a free place to share photos with friends, and earn from the audience instead of paper.

Uploads are free, albums are easy to share, and friends comment on each other's photos. Within a few years, Kodak owns the place where families keep their pictures, just as phones start getting cameras.
You followed the customer's new habit, sharing, even though it hurt print sales. Owning the audience is worth more than owning the paper.
Kodak cameras fly off the shelves and the brand looks modern again. But every competitor is selling cameras too, and prices fall every year.

Cameras were a real business, but a crowded one with thin margins. You gave up the part of digital that customers come back to every day. What would have worked: Keep the website and make it about sharing. That's where people would spend their time.
It's 2007. Film sales are collapsing across the industry, but your digital businesses are growing fast enough to carry the company. You have a strong hand. Don't waste it.
It's 2007. Film sales are collapsing. Your digital business is real but not yet big enough to replace what film used to earn. This is your last big decision.
It's 2007. Film sales are falling fast. This is your last chance to save the company.
You have patents, chemistry expertise, factories and a famous name. Film won't come back.
Where do you bet the company's future?
Whatever we pick, we can only afford to do it properly once.
You win shelf space, then lose money on every price cut. Within a few years, the phone in everyone's pocket takes good enough pictures, and the standalone camera market starts to shrink.

You chose a market where prices only go down and a bigger threat, the phone, was already arriving. What would have worked: Use what Kodak is best at, chemistry and materials, to enter new growing markets.

In February 2007 Kodak unveiled EasyShare all-in-one printers, claiming its ink could cut the cost of printing a photo by up to half. They went on sale in March. The printers never became the big new business Kodak needed.

Cheaper ink was a smart pitch for a shrinking habit. You bet on people printing photos at home just as they started keeping them on screens. What would have worked: Use Kodak's chemistry and materials know-how to enter new growing markets, as Fujifilm did.

You cut costs hard in film, then point your chemists at medical imaging, specialty films and materials. It's painful and slow, but new businesses start replacing what film used to earn. Fujifilm made a similar move and is still thriving.
You asked what Kodak was really good at, chemistry and materials, instead of what it used to sell. Skills travel to new markets; products don't.
By 2012, Kodak is a digital imaging and materials company. Film is a small, profitable corner of the business. Business schools teach your story as the incumbent that disrupted itself.
Kodak shrinks a lot, but it never goes bankrupt. You fixed enough, late enough, to keep the lights on. With a few earlier calls, it could have led the digital age.

On January 19, 2012, Kodak files for bankruptcy. That April, Facebook buys Instagram, a photo-sharing app with 13 employees, for one billion dollars. The company that invented the digital camera lost the digital age.
Three bad calls. The board loses faith and replaces you. Your successor inherits a company that's falling behind, and the clock is still ticking.
You run Nestlé India. Maggi is the country's favourite instant noodles, a two-minute meal in millions of kitchens and hostel rooms. It makes up about 30% of your company's sales.

Food safety officers in Barabanki, Uttar Pradesh, picked up a Maggi batch for a routine check. A state lab now reports lead at 17.2 ppm, against a limit of 2 ppm. It also found MSG, though your pack says no added MSG.
How do you respond to the report?
This is one batch in one district. But how you treat one batch tells people how you'll treat the next.
Nestlé appealed and asked for the samples to go to the central referral lab in Kolkata. That lab confirmed the findings. The problem did not go away. It grew.

Using the proper appeal was your right. But treating it only as a legal step left the public question, about the label and the lead, unanswered. What would have worked: Appeal if you disagree, but also fix the label and order fresh independent tests, then tell the public what you found.
Our estimate: the batch disappears, but the lab report doesn't. When it comes out later, saying nothing looks like hiding.
Silence feels safe until the news comes out. Then it looks like you had something to hide. What would have worked: Act in the open: test independently, fix the label, and tell people what you found.
Our estimate: it costs money and some awkward headlines, but when other states start testing, you already have your own independent results to show.
Being open early builds a store of trust you can draw on when things get worse.

April 2015. Uttar Pradesh orders a recall of a batch made in February 2014. Nestlé says that batch had already passed its best-before date. Other states start testing. Delhi reports that 10 of 13 samples are above its limit and bans sales for 15 days. On 3 June, Nestlé India's shares fall about 10%, their biggest one-day drop in nine years.
Your own independent tests are already public, but the bans are spreading state by state. Parents are worried.
The bans are spreading state by state. Big shops are asking whether to keep Maggi on their shelves. Parents are worried.
What do you say and do?
You may be right about the science. The question is what worried parents need from you this week.

Nestlé said more than 1,000 batches had been tested and lead was within limits, and that only Uttar Pradesh had ordered a recall. More states banned sales, and big shops and the Indian army dropped Maggi. Many critics called the response slow.

You answered fear with numbers. Even if the numbers were right, parents heard a company protecting its sales. What would have worked: Take the product off the shelves yourself, say safety comes first, and let the tests speak later.
Our estimate: sales stop overnight and the cost is huge. But because you acted first, people see a company that puts their families first.
Putting safety ahead of sales, before anyone forced you, protects the one thing a food brand can't buy back: trust.
Our estimate: you follow each ban as it comes, but every new state makes headlines, and it looks like you only act when forced.
Following the rules state by state is reasonable, but it lets the crisis set the pace instead of you. What would have worked: Make one clear move yourself across the whole country.
Our estimate: the empty shelves make the news, but so does your choice. Then the national food regulator orders a recall of all approved Maggi variants and calls them unsafe.

On 5 June 2015, Nestlé announced it was withdrawing Maggi from shelves across India. The same day, the national food regulator ordered a recall of all nine approved variants and called them unsafe. About 38,000 tonnes of noodles were destroyed, burned in cement plants. Nestlé India reported a loss of Rs 64.4 crore for the quarter.
The regulator's order covers all nine variants, including ones that were never tested. You believe the testing process was unfair.
What do you do about the ban?
You can be right in court and still lose in people's kitchens. Think about both.

Nestlé challenged the order in the Bombay High Court. In August 2015 the court set the ban aside. It found that Nestlé had not been given a fair hearing, that the labs used were not accredited, and that the ban covered variants never tested. It ordered new tests in three accredited labs. The regulator later appealed to the Supreme Court.
You challenged the process, not the people, and asked for fair tests. That gave you a clear, public way back.
Our estimate: the ads make the fight personal. Officials dig in, and many people now see a big company bullying its regulator.
Attacking the people who keep food safe looks like you don't care about safety. What would have worked: Use the courts to ask for a fair process, and keep your public message about safety.
Our estimate: you avoid a public fight, but with no clear process for retesting, the noodles stay off the shelves for much longer.
Calm was good, but without a fair process to ask for, you had no clear way back. What would have worked: Respectfully ask a court for a fair process and accredited retests.
October 2015. All 90 samples in the court-ordered tests have come back clear, and three factories have started making Maggi again.
The noodles are cleared to return. You have one chance to win families back.
How do you bring Maggi back?
Coming back is not just restocking shelves. It is asking families to trust you again.
Our estimate: a new name confuses loyal fans and looks like you are hiding from Maggi's past.

Your brand's history is also its strength. Running from it throws away years of love. What would have worked: Bring Maggi back under its own name, carefully, once new batches have also passed the tests.
Our estimate: sales jump back quickly, but one bad test on a rushed batch could start the whole crisis again.
Speed brings sales back, but trust needs proof before volume. What would have worked: Wait until new batches also pass the tests, then return with a big, careful launch.
Nestlé waited until new batches also cleared the tests. On 9 November 2015, around Diwali, Maggi went back on sale in 100 cities, with an online shopping partner.
You came back with proof first and then a big, warm moment, giving families a reason to try Maggi again.
Our estimate: because you put families first from the start, Maggi comes back with its fans' trust intact and soon wins back almost all of the market.

Maggi came back. By October 2016 Nestlé put its share of instant noodles at 57%, against 75% before the crisis, with new rivals now on the shelf. In 2024 the national consumer commission dismissed the government's case after a central lab found lead within limits.
Our estimate: the noodles come back, but families have moved on to rival brands, and Maggi never wins back its old place.
Our estimate: after three costly calls in a row, the board loses its trust in you and asks someone else to lead the company through the crisis.
It is 2000. You run Netflix, a small company that rents DVDs by post. You are losing money. Meanwhile Blockbuster, the giant of movie rental, earns about $800 million a year from late fees alone.
Money is tight. Blockbuster has stores everywhere and cash to spare. You could ask them to buy you and run their online rental for them.
What do you do?
There is no shame in looking for a safe harbour. Just don't give up on what you are building.

The founders offered to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for $50 million, and Blockbuster said no. Netflix kept growing its flat monthly fee and no-late-fee service, and reached 1 million subscribers within about three years.

Looking for a buyer was a sensible hedge for a small company losing money. But it could have handed your idea to a company that did not believe in it. What would have worked: Raise money from investors who believe in the idea, and keep control of what you are building.
Our estimate: you survive, but slowly. While you wait, others start renting DVDs online too.
Shrinking a young company saves money but stops the learning that makes it valuable. What would have worked: Keep building, and raise money from people who believe in the idea.
Our estimate: raising money is hard in a bad year, but you keep control. You keep growing the no-late-fee service that customers love.
You protected the thing that made you special, a model customers loved, instead of handing it to a rival.

It is 2006. Netflix went public in 2002, with over 500,000 subscribers, a $19.95 monthly plan and no late fees. Blockbuster launched its own online service in 2004, and now it lets members return DVDs in its stores. By the end of 2006 you have 6 million subscribers.
Your DVD business is strong, with more than 70,000 titles to choose from. Internet speeds are getting better, but watching movies online is still new and clumsy.
What do you do about streaming?
The DVD business is paying the bills. The question is how long it will keep doing that.
Our estimate: profits look good for a few years, but when streaming takes off, others are ready and you are not.
Waiting for a technology to be perfect means a rival learns it first. What would have worked: Start streaming now, even small, and learn while the DVD business pays the bills.
Our estimate: a few keen fans pay extra, but most members never try it, so you learn slowly.
Charging for something new and clumsy keeps most people from trying it. What would have worked: Give streaming away free inside existing plans so every member tries it.
In January 2007 Netflix added instant streaming on computers at no extra charge, with about 1,000 titles. How many hours you could watch depended on your plan.
Making streaming free meant every member tried it. You started moving customers to the future while the DVD business still paid the bills.

It is 2010. Blockbuster has gone bankrupt, and Netflix has 20 million subscribers. In November you added a $7.99 streaming-only plan and raised the price of DVD plans. Netflix made $160 million in profit this year.
Streaming is taking off and you are behind. Every show you offer belongs to someone else, and they can take it away.
Almost everything you stream belongs to movie studios and TV networks. They can raise their prices or take shows away. A new political drama is looking for a home.
Do you start paying for your own shows?
TV networks usually test a pilot first. You do not have to play by their rules.
Our estimate: costs stay low for a while, but studios raise prices each year and keep their best shows for their own services.
If everything you sell belongs to someone else, they decide your future. What would have worked: Own some of your shows, so you have something no one can take away.
Our estimate: you play it safe, but the show's makers want a full commitment, and a TV network wins the deal.
Playing by the old rules made you an ordinary bidder. Bold makers want a partner who commits. What would have worked: Commit to a full series without a pilot and win the show.
In March 2011 Netflix outbid HBO and AMC for a new drama called House of Cards and ordered two seasons, 26 episodes, without a pilot. The show would not be ready for almost two years.
You made a big bet on owning something no one else could offer, and you won it by committing more than the old players would.

It is July 2011. Your stock is near its highest ever, close to $304 a share. You want to push members toward streaming and buy more shows to stream. Members who want both DVDs and streaming pay about $10 a month.
How do you change your plans?
Members will forgive a change they understand. They hate a surprise in their bill.
Our estimate: a few members grumble, but most stay. You get more money for new shows without a shock.
Small, well-explained changes keep trust while still moving the business forward.

Netflix made DVDs and streaming separate plans at $7.99 each. Members who wanted both now paid about $16 instead of about $10. Many were angry, and in September Netflix lowered its forecast of how many subscribers it would have.
A 60% price rise all at once felt like a betrayal to loyal members. What would have worked: Raise prices slowly and explain why, so members feel part of the change instead of punished by it.
Our estimate: many members who still love DVDs leave, and you lose money you need for new shows.

The direction was right, but cutting off a business customers still used was too fast. What would have worked: Keep DVDs while they still earn money, and move people to streaming with price and better shows.
It is September 2011. Members are cancelling and your stock is falling. You think the plan is right, but people feel ignored.
It is September 2011. You want DVDs and streaming to be two different businesses, each with its own focus.
What do you do with the DVD business?
When customers are angry, ask first what they actually need from you.

Netflix's CEO apologized for poor communication and said DVDs would move to a new brand called Qwikster, with its own website. People mocked the name, and by October Netflix shares had lost more than half their value since July.

Members asked for one simple service. You gave them two websites and two bills, right when they were already upset. What would have worked: Listen first: keep one website and one account, and explain clearly why prices changed.
Our estimate: the anger cools down. Some members leave, but most stay, because the service still feels simple.
When trust is hurt, simple and honest beats clever.
Our estimate: members calm down, but you lose the money you needed for new shows, and investors wonder if you have a plan.
Rolling everything back fixes the anger but gives up a strategy that was right in direction. What would have worked: Keep the strategy, fix how it was done: one account, clear communication.
It is October 2011. Everyone is laughing at the name Qwikster, and your stock keeps falling. You have weeks, not months.
What now?
Admitting a mistake fast is cheaper than defending it slowly.
Our estimate: more members leave, and the fight distracts everyone from building the streaming service.
Defending a mistake because you announced it only makes it bigger. What would have worked: Drop the part customers hated quickly, and keep the part that serves the long-term plan.

Within weeks Netflix dropped Qwikster and kept one website and one account, but kept the new prices. In the July to September quarter its US subscribers had fallen from 24.6 million to 23.8 million, and Netflix said the price rise had hurt more than the name.

Backing down fast on the confusing part was smart. Keeping the prices gave you money for new shows, but cost you members. What would have worked: Fix the mistake quickly, and pair the higher price with something members can see, like new shows.
Our estimate: loyal members feel heard and come back. You have less money for shows this year, but trust is restored.
You fixed both the confusion and the shock, and showed members their loyalty mattered.

On February 1, 2013, Netflix released all 13 episodes of House of Cards on the same day. That quarter it added 2 million US streaming members, reaching 29.2 million, and its shares jumped 24% after the results.
Our estimate: you moved early to streaming and kept your members' trust. Netflix becomes the place people go to watch.
Our estimate: Netflix survives the storm, but rivals have caught up, and you spend years winning back what you lost.
Our estimate: you waited too long or lost your members' trust. A rival becomes the home of streaming, and Netflix fades like the company it once beat.
Our estimate: after three costly calls in a row, the board loses its trust in you and asks someone else to lead Netflix.
It is the end of 2007. Nokia sold 435 million phones this year. Four in every ten phones sold in the world are yours, and India is one of your biggest markets.

Your Symbian software runs on more than half of all smartphones. You own about half of the company that makes it. But a new rival is coming: Google's Android. And a year ago, a phone with a big touchscreen arrived.
What do you do with your smartphone software?
Symbian is winning today. The question is whether it can win the next five years.

Nokia paid about €264 million for the rest of Symbian and planned to open its code to everyone through a new Symbian Foundation. It now owned all of the most popular smartphone software. But it was software from before the touchscreen era.

Owning Symbian gave you control, but it was control of yesterday's software. Giving it away did not make it better for touchscreens. What would have worked: Keep Symbian for cheap phones, but start a new, touch-first software team now and give it the best people.
Our estimate: you save money this year, but your phones start to look old in shop windows. Buyers with money to spend begin to choose touchscreens instead.

Rich buyers set the trend that everyone else follows a few years later. Calling a new product a fad is how leaders get left behind. What would have worked: Take the touchscreen seriously and build software made for it, even if today's phones still sell well.
Our estimate: a small team builds new touch software while Symbian keeps paying the bills. It costs money and causes fights inside the company, but by 2010 you have a modern phone ready.
You protected today's business and built tomorrow's at the same time, with a team that was free to break old habits.
Our estimate: it is late 2010, and your new touch phones keep you in the race. But by the end of the year Apple has 16% of smartphone sales, and the board wants a clear plan for the future.

It is late 2010. Your share of smartphones has fallen from almost half in 2007 to 30.8%, while Apple now has 16%. You and Intel have joined forces on new software called MeeGo, but only plans exist so far. In September the board brought in a new CEO from Microsoft. That CEO is you.
Samsung, LG and HTC all use Google's Android. Microsoft wants a big partner for its phone software, which has only 3.4% of smartphone sales. Your own MeeGo software is still not finished.
Which software will power your smartphones?
Whatever you choose, choose fast. Every month you wait, buyers move on.
Our estimate: you keep full control, but the software arrives late and few app makers want to build for a fourth platform. Your phones are beautiful, but their app stores are empty.

Owning your software is powerful only if developers build for it. Arriving late with a new platform is a hard climb. What would have worked: Join the platform where the apps and buyers already are, and compete on hardware, price and reach.
Our estimate: your first Android phones arrive within a year. With the world's best supply chain and shops in every town, you sell them at every price, and buyers who left start coming back.
When a platform has already won, the smart move is to use it and compete where you are strongest: making, pricing and selling phones everywhere.

In February 2011 Nokia made Windows Phone its main smartphone software and pushed Symbian and MeeGo aside. Its share price fell 9.5% that morning. Nokia said Android would turn it into just another phone maker and give Google too much of the money from services. The first Windows phones, the Lumia 800 and 710, only arrived in October 2011.

You tied your future to software that very few people used, and it took months before you had anything new to sell. What would have worked: Choose the platform buyers and app makers had already chosen, and fight on hardware, price and distribution.

Your new smartphones are still on the way, and India is slipping. You once had about 70% of India's phone market, but your share has fallen for nine quarters in a row. About half of Indian buyers want phones that take two SIM cards, and local brands sell them cheap.

India is your biggest test. You once had about 70% of its phone market, but your share has fallen for nine quarters in a row. About half of Indian buyers want phones that take two SIM cards, and local brands sell them cheap.
How do you fight for India?
Indian buyers are not asking for your fanciest phone. Listen to what they are asking for.
Our estimate: local brands and Samsung take the cheap and middle market, which is most of India. Your shops still show your name, but fewer people walk out with your phone.

In a price-sensitive market, the cheap phone is how a customer meets your brand. Give it away and you lose them for years. What would have worked: Give Indian buyers what they asked for: cheap, tough phones with two SIM slots, sold through the shops you already have.
Our estimate: some buyers trade up, but most Indian phone buyers still want a cheap phone with two SIM slots. You win a little and lose a lot of margin.

Cutting prices helps, but it does not fix the real gap: the phone buyers wanted was not on your shelf. What would have worked: Build the cheap, dual-SIM phones buyers were asking for, and keep smartphone prices for later.

In June 2011 Nokia launched dual-SIM phones in India. It also sold its new Asha phones for about Rs 3,000 to 8,000 and gave shops more margin. Its share of phones shipped in India still fell, from 31% in 2011 to 22.2% in the first half of 2012, but Nokia stayed number one.
You listened to what Indian buyers wanted and used your biggest strength, the shops that already sold your phones everywhere.

Our estimate: it is 2013, your Android phones sell well, but the fight with Samsung is tough and margins are thin. Meanwhile your network equipment business, Nokia Siemens Networks, quietly makes good money.

It is 2013. At the end of 2012 Samsung sold 22.7% of the world's phones and Nokia 18%. Symbian is down to 1.2% of smartphone sales. Your phone business made €14.9 billion in sales in 2012, but it lost over €1 billion. Your network equipment business, Nokia Siemens Networks, is doing much better.
Nokia Siemens Networks builds the equipment that mobile networks run on. In 2012 it made €822 million in adjusted operating profit. Your partner, Siemens, wants to sell its half.
What do you do with the networks business?
Sometimes your future is already inside the company. You just have not been looking at it.
Our estimate: you get a big cheque, but it disappears into a phone business that keeps losing money. Now you have no strong business left to fall back on.
You sold your healthiest business to feed your weakest one. That buys time, not a future. What would have worked: Keep the business that makes money and has a future, even if it is less famous.

In July 2013 Nokia agreed to buy Siemens' half of Nokia Siemens Networks for €1.7 billion. Nokia's shares rose more than 7% that day. The deal used a lot of cash: Nokia's net cash was expected to drop to about €2.0 to 2.5 billion.
You spent money to fully own the part of the company that was profitable and had a future, even while the famous part was in trouble.
Our estimate: you raise some cash and keep part of the profits, but you no longer control the business that could become Nokia's future.

It was a safe middle path, but it gave away control of your best asset at the moment you needed it most. What would have worked: Take full control of the profitable networks business and build the company's future around it.
Our estimate: your Android phones are holding their own, but Samsung is bigger and the price war never stops. Now Microsoft is ready to buy your whole phone business.
Your phone business is losing over €1 billion a year. Microsoft, your software partner, is ready to buy your whole phone business.
What do you do with the phone business that made Nokia famous?
The name on the phone is not the same as the company. Ask what keeps Nokia alive.
Our estimate: you keep the famous phones, but the losses keep growing and eat the cash your other businesses need.

Pride in what made you famous can stop you from protecting what keeps you alive. What would have worked: Sell the losing business while it is still worth a lot, and put the company's future into what works.

In September 2013 Nokia agreed to sell its phone business to Microsoft for €5.44 billion, including €1.65 billion for a licence to its patents. About 32,000 staff moved to Microsoft. Nokia kept its networks business, its HERE maps and its patents.
You let go of what made Nokia famous to save what could keep Nokia alive, and you sold while the business was still worth billions.
Our estimate: the switch helps a little, but you are years behind Samsung, and the phone business keeps losing money while you catch up.
It was the right platform, but two years too late. Late fixes cost more and win less. What would have worked: Either move to the winning platform early, or sell the business while it still has value.
Our estimate: with early Android phones, shops in every town and cheap phones India wanted, Nokia stays one of the world's top phone makers. Your network business grows alongside it.
Our estimate: you moved early and listened to buyers. Nokia stays a leader, in phones or in the networks that carry their calls.

In April 2014 the sale to Microsoft closed. Nokia became mainly a networks company, with HERE maps and its patents, led by the head of its networks business. The phones that made it famous now belonged to someone else, but Nokia itself survived.
Our estimate: you held on to the past for too long. With the phones losing money and no strong business left to fall back on, Nokia becomes a story people tell about how leaders fall.
Three costly calls in a row. The board has lost its trust in you and asks someone else to lead Nokia through the storm.
You sell books online in India. But few Indians use credit cards. Couriers that collect cash for you take weeks to pay you, and they charge high fees.
How do you let people pay?
Our estimate: the few people with cards buy from you, but most of India never tries your shop.
If most customers can't pay your way, you have shut the door on them. What would have worked: Let customers pay cash at the door, and build your own delivery so the cash comes back fast.

Flipkart offered cash on delivery and started its own delivery arm as a pilot in December 2010, because it did not want outside couriers holding its cash. That arm, eKart, later grew to serve over 800 cities.
Customers who didn't trust online shopping could see the product first. And owning delivery meant your cash came back quickly.
Our estimate: more people buy, but your money is stuck with couriers for weeks, and you run short of cash.
You solved the customer's problem but created a cash problem for yourself. What would have worked: Offer cash on delivery and run your own delivery, so the cash reaches you fast.
You make washing powder at home. The big brand, Surf, sells at Rs 13 a kilo.
How do you price your powder?
Our estimate: shoppers pick the famous brand at the same price, and your powder stays on the shelf.
Against a famous brand, a similar price gives buyers no reason to switch. What would have worked: Price far below Surf for families who could never afford it, and sell to them directly.
Our estimate: you build a small, loyal following, but growth is slow.
Starting small is safe, but it leaves the huge market below Surf's price for someone else. What would have worked: Go after that huge market directly, with a very low price and door-to-door selling.
The founder priced Nirma at Rs 3.50 a kilo and sold it door to door by bicycle. Nirma became India's largest-selling detergent within a decade, and Surf was badly hurt.
Millions of families wanted washing powder but could not afford the big brand. You built a product for them.
Seven people near Chicago have died after taking Tylenol capsules that someone had laced with poison. The capsules were sold in Chicago-area stores. Tylenol has 35% of its market.
Our estimate: you save money, but people across the country stay afraid and stop buying.

Fear does not stay inside one city. A small recall looks like you care more about money than safety. What would have worked: Recall every bottle across the country, and come back with packaging that can't be tampered with.

Johnson & Johnson recalled 31 million bottles across the US, at a cost of $100 million. Tylenol's share fell to 7%. After it came back in tamper-proof packaging, it returned to 35% by the end of 1983.
You put customer safety above short-term money, and customers trusted you again.
Our estimate: while you wait, more people stop trusting the brand, and every day of silence makes it worse.
When lives are at risk, waiting looks like you don't care. What would have worked: Act at once: recall everything, then fix the packaging.
Your software company in Chennai needs programmers. You could compete for graduates from top colleges. But you believe young people without degrees could do as well with training.
How do you find talent?
Our estimate: you hire good people, but the cost keeps rising and many leave for bigger offers.
Competing on salary alone is a race where the richest company wins. What would have worked: Train your own talent from people others overlook.

In 2004 the company, then called AdventNet and now Zoho, started what became Zoho University: a two-year course for Class 12 students. Students pay no fees and get Rs 10,000 a month. Most are hired by Zoho, and many come from low-income, often rural, families.
You found talent where others weren't looking, and trained it the way your company works.
Our estimate: work gets done, but you never build your own skilled team, and quality is hard to control.
For a software company, the people who write the code are the business. What would have worked: Build your own team, even if it means training people yourself.
Shampoo is sold in bottles. Your family has already tried selling products in small, cheap packets.
How do you sell your shampoo?
Our estimate: you fight the big brands on their ground, with less money, and lose.
Copying the leader's pack and price gives poorer buyers no new reason to try you. What would have worked: Make a pack small enough for the customer's pocket.
Our estimate: a few more people can afford it, but you still miss the villages and small towns.
Smaller helped, but not small enough for the biggest group of buyers. What would have worked: Go all the way down to a single-use packet at a tiny price, sold in rural shops.

The founder's company, then called Beauty Products and later renamed CavinKare, launched Chik shampoo in 10 ml packets in 1983, at a very low price, and pushed it in rural markets. Within a couple of years Chik became the top shampoo in South India.
You made the product fit what customers could pay each day, not what the big brands wanted to sell.
Your startup lets people stay in strangers' homes. Investor after investor has said no, and the business needs money to survive.
Our estimate: you are safe, but you will never know if the idea could have worked.

Many good ideas look bad to investors at first. Quitting early ends the test before it starts. What would have worked: Find a creative way to raise a little cash and keep going long enough to prove the idea.
Our estimate: you survive a few more months, but the debt grows and nothing proves the idea to anyone.
Debt buys time but does not show anyone why they should believe in you. What would have worked: Raise cash in a way that also shows your grit and creativity.
The founders designed and sold election-themed cereal boxes at $40 each and raised about $30,000. The hustle impressed the startup programme Y Combinator, which accepted them and invested $20,000.
You kept the company alive and showed investors exactly the kind of grit they look for.
A government-owned company rules India's watch market, mainly with mechanical watches that need winding. Quartz watches are a newer technology.
What kind of watches do you make?
Our estimate: you become a smaller copy of the leader, just as the market starts moving to quartz.
Copying the leader's old technology means you arrive late to the future. What would have worked: Build only for the new technology, quartz.

Titan, a joint venture of Tata and TIDCO, a Tamil Nadu government agency, made only quartz watches. Its first range sold at Rs 350 to 900. The old leader, HMT, went into slow decline, and Titan held over 60% of India's organised watch market by 2012.
You built for where the technology was going, not where it had been.
Our estimate: you cover both markets, but your quartz watches don't stand out, and your mechanical ones fade.
Hedging felt safe, but it split your effort just when one side was winning. What would have worked: Commit fully to quartz and be the best at it.

It is October 2003. Worms have been found in your chocolates in Maharashtra. At first you defended your factory and said you could not watch every shop. The regulator moved to prosecute, and sales are falling.
What do you do now?
Our estimate: you may be right about the shops, but parents keep away, and the story stays in the news.

Even if you are right, blaming others does not make a parent feel safe buying chocolate for a child. What would have worked: Fix the problem you can control, like the packaging, and show customers the fix.
Our estimate: some buyers return for the discount, but the worry stays, and cheap prices make the brand look desperate.
A discount fixes price, but the problem was trust. What would have worked: Fix the packaging and show people how you make your chocolate.
Cadbury improved its packaging and ran ads in which a famous film star visited the factory. Sales, which had fallen after the news, recovered.
You fixed what you could control and let customers see it for themselves.
You make Surf, India's leading washing powder. A cheap new powder called Nirma is winning huge numbers of customers who never bought Surf, and now some who did.
How do you respond?
Our estimate: Nirma keeps growing, and by the time you act, it is the biggest name in the market.
Cheap rivals start with customers you don't want, then move up to the ones you do. What would have worked: Launch your own low-price brand early, and keep Surf as the premium one.
Hindustan Lever launched a low-cost brand, Wheel, to fight Nirma. But its answer came only after a long delay. The shock changed how Unilever sold in poorer markets, including selling small packets.
A second, cheaper brand let you fight on price without cutting Surf's. The mistake was waiting so long.
Our estimate: you win some buyers back, but your profits fall and Surf starts to look ordinary.
Cutting the price of your premium brand damages it to fight a battle it wasn't built for. What would have worked: Fight with a separate cheaper brand, and keep Surf premium.
Tata Tea grows tea but wants to own famous tea brands. Its first try to buy the British brand Tetley, the world's second-biggest tea company, failed for lack of money. Now there is another chance.
Do you borrow heavily to buy a famous global brand?
Our estimate: you grow abroad step by step, but it takes many years and a lot of advertising to become known.
Building a global brand from zero is slow and costly. What would have worked: Buy a famous brand that can earn enough to repay the loan.
Our estimate: you grow more tea, but you stay a seller of a raw product while others earn the brand profits.
More gardens make you bigger in the low-profit part of the business. What would have worked: Move into brands, where the profits are.
In 2000 Tata Tea bought Tetley for £271 million, a deal funded largely by borrowing. Tetley became Tata's main global brand, and about two-thirds of Tata Tea's sales later came from the Tetley Group.
You bought what you could not build quickly, and got a famous global brand in one step.
It is early 2008. Your company believes Starbucks has lost its way in its US stores. Your returning CEO has a plan that includes better staff training.
How do you retrain thousands of baristas?

On 26 February 2008, Starbucks closed nearly 7,100 US stores for one evening to retrain baristas. Many called it a gimmick. Starbucks also closed about 600 weak US stores, and its profit fell sharply that year. By 2010 it posted record results, after a turnaround that included much more than the training evening.
Closing every store showed staff and customers that quality mattered more than one night of sales.
Our estimate: training happens, but slowly, and nobody notices that anything has changed.
Quiet training works, but a turnaround also needs everyone to see that you are serious. What would have worked: Make one big, visible move that shows staff and customers quality comes first.
Our estimate: busy staff watch them when they can, and service stays the same.
Cheap training sends the message that training doesn't matter. What would have worked: Invest real time in training, together, so the change sticks.
Your company sells a cheap energy drink, Tzinga, at Rs 25 against Red Bull's Rs 95. One day a co-founder brings aam panna to work, and it gives the team an idea.
What do you bet on next?
Our estimate: sales rise a little, but you are still fighting giants in a market they own.
More ads for a me-too product rarely beat a famous brand. What would have worked: Sell something customers love but can't find in shops.
Our estimate: you get on the shelf, but your juices look like everyone else's.
Copying the big brands' products gives shoppers no reason to choose you. What would have worked: Bottle the traditional Indian drinks people grew up with.
Hector Beverages launched Paper Boat drinks in Delhi and Bengaluru in August 2013, in pouches that cost less to make than cartons. By 2015 Paper Boat made about 90% of the company's sales.
You sold something customers already loved but couldn't buy in shops.
Your low-cost online share trading company, founded in 2010, made a profit in its second year. You could raise money from investors to grow faster.
Do you take investor money?
Our estimate: you grow faster, but you now answer to investors who want even faster growth, and costs climb.
Investor money speeds things up, but it brings pressure that a profitable company may not need. What would have worked: If customers already pay you well, grow from your own profits and keep control.

Zerodha stayed bootstrapped and avoided big ad spending, because its founder did not want to answer to investors. In 2023-24 it made a profit of about Rs 4,700 crore on Rs 8,320 crore of revenue, still without outside investors.
A profitable business that customers love can fund its own growth and keep control.
Our estimate: you grow, but the loan payments eat into your profits every month, and one bad year could hurt badly.
Debt adds risk to a business that didn't need it. What would have worked: Grow from the profits you already make.
Food delivery is a race for speed. You could promise food in 10 minutes. Critics warn it could push delivery riders to ride unsafely.

Zomato announced Zomato Instant in March 2022 and tried it in Gurugram, saying riders would not be punished for late orders. But daily orders were too low to cover the fixed costs. By February 2023 it was relaunched as Zomato Everyday, home-style meals from Rs 89.

A bold promise got headlines, but daily orders were too low to cover the fixed costs of running it. What would have worked: Test quietly with a few users and prove each order can make money before making big promises.
Our estimate: you learn how much each fast order really costs before anyone knows, and only grow it if it makes money.
Quiet tests let you fail cheaply and learn the real numbers.
Our estimate: fewer headlines, but riders stay safe and customers still get fast food.
A realistic promise is easier to keep, but it doesn't stand out. What would have worked: Test a faster option quietly, and only promise it when the numbers work.
